newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Germany's Deutz aims for operating breakeven.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Germany's Deutz aims for operating breakeven.

text.p: Deutz AG, the German motor maker risen from the wreckage of Kloeckner-Humboldt-Deutz AG, said on Tuesday it returned to net profit in 1996 after a bailout, and its operating results would break even this year.

Chairman Anton Schneider told a news conference that the company made a net profit of 874 million marks ($505.9 million) in 1996, after a net loss of 1.134 billion marks the year before. The profit resulted entirely from 897 million marks in extraordinaries, mainly banks' contributions to last year's rescue.

Schneider said the company made an operating loss of 56 million marks in 1996, but there would be no losses in 1997, and 1998 would show further improvement as the company continued to restructure, shedding subsidiaries and focusing solely on motors.

"Our strategy is very clear: motors, motors, motors," Schneider said of the company, which makes a wide range of motors for construction equipment, pumps and compressors as well as cars, trucks and buses.

The industrial plant activities that it plans to sell accounted for about one-third of its 1996 sales and workforce. It aims to lower its overheads while boosting activities in Asia, North America and Latin America.

Deutz is now holding talks with potential buyers for its environmental technology and Indumont units, and hopes to sell them by June 30. Indumont builds, services and maintains industrial plants, particularly in pipeline and conveyor systems. The company aims to sell its cement technology and raw materials processing activities by the end of the year.

It also still plans to sell its KHD Humboldt Wedag unit, whose contracts for three Saudi cement plants were the source of the original losses that led to the one-billion-mark bailout by the company's creditor banks led by Deutsche Bank AG.
One of the three plants has been completed and delivered. A second is to be finished by June 30, and the third by the end of October.

Deutz plans to propose a 9.15 million mark capital increase at its June 26 annual shareholders' meeting. The share issue, in three equal tranches from 1998 to 2000, will go to management and employees at favourable prices in return for the salary cuts they accepted as part of the rescue.
Management's participation in the share plan will be dependent on the degree to which Deutz shares outperform the Frankfurt DAX share index, Schneider said.

The company said the bank bailout had cost 1.008 billion marks. It said it had reduced its net debt to 602 million marks by the end of 1996 from 1.023 billion marks a year earlier, and that it had capital of 220 million marks.
Sales in 1996 were 2.921 billion marks, down from 3.285 billion marks, while debt was reduced to 602 million marks from 1.023 billion marks.
Sales in the first four months of 1997 rose to 858 million marks, up 17 percent from a year earlier.
Incoming orders in the four months were 901 million marks, down from 999 million marks in the year-earlier period.
The company has tax-loss carryforwards totaling 2.4 billion marks, which it hopes to apply toward its own profits in coming years, Schneider said.
